'''Men's studies''' is an [[interdisciplinary]] [[academic field]] devoted to topics concerning [[men]], [[masculinity]], [[gender]], [[culture]], [[politics]] and [[Human sexuality|sexuality]]. It academically examines what it means to be a man in contemporary society.<ref>{{Cite news |last= Bennett|first=Jessica |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/09/fashion/masculinities-studies-stonybrook-michael-kimmel.html?_r=0|title=A master's degree in...masculinity?|date=August 8, 2015|work=[[New York Times]]}}</ref>

== Origins ==
Sociologists and psychologists in the [[Nordic countries]] such as Norwegians [[Erik Grønseth]] and [[Per Olav Tiller]] were early pioneers of men's studies as a research field; Grønseth and Tiller's classic study of [[father absence]] in sailor families and its impact on children's [[personality development]] in the 1950s is often regarded as the starting point of men's studies in the Nordic countries.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Mannsforskning |encyclopedia=[[Store norske leksikon]] |year=2018 |url=https://snl.no/mannsforskning }}</ref>

In Anglophone countries, men's studies was formed, largely in response to an emerging [[men's rights]] movement,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wootton |first1=Nancy A. |title=The men's movement and men's studies: a study of the literature |journal=RQ |date=Winter 1993 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=183–194 |id={{Gale|A14769920}} |jstor=20862406 }}</ref> and as such, has been taught in academic settings only since the 1970s.<ref name=":1" />
 
In contrast to the discipline of masculine psychology, men's studies programs and courses often include contemporary discussions of men's rights, [[feminist theory]], [[queer theory]], [[matriarchy]], [[patriarchy]], and more generally, what proponents describe as the social, historical, and cultural influences on the constructions of [[Man|men]]. They often discuss the issues surrounding [[male privilege]], seen as evolving into more subtle and covert forms rather than disappearing in the modern era.{{Citation needed|date=February 2020}}

It is important to distinguish the specific approach often defined as Critical Studies on Men. This approach was largely developed in the anglophone countries from the early 1980s - especially in the United Kingdom -  centred then around the work of Jeff Hearn, David Morgan and colleagues.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book|editor1=Hearn, Jeff |editor2=Morgan, David|title=Men, masculinities & social theory|publisher=Unwin Hyman|year=1990|location=London}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> The influence of the approach has spread globally since then. It is inspired primarily by a range of feminist perspectives (including socialist and radical) and places emphasis on the need for research and practice to explicitly challenge men's and boys' sexism.<ref name=":8" /> Although it explores a very broad range of men's practices, it tends to focus especially on issues related to sexuality and/or men's violences.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=The Violences of Men: How Men Talk About and How Agencies Respond to Men's Violence to Women |date=1998 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-0-8039-7940-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Although originally largely rooted in sociology, it has since engaged with a broad range of other disciplines including social policy, social work, cultural studies, gender studies, education and law.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203413067 |title=International Encyclopedia of Men and Masculinities |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-134-31707-3 |editor-last1=Flood |editor-last2=Kegan Gardiner |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Michael |editor-first2=Judith |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In more recent years, Critical Studies on Men research has made particular use of comparative and/or transnational perspectives.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=Men of the World: Genders, Globalizations, Transnational Times |date=2015 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-1-4739-2677-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230626447 |title=European Perspectives on Men and Masculinities |year=2006 |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |last2=Pringle |first2=Keith |isbn=978-0-230-59447-0 |url=http://www.palgrave.com/us/book/9781403918130 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230338005 |title=Men and Masculinities Around the World |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-349-29067-3 |editor-last1=Ruspini |editor-last2=Hearn |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Elisabetta |editor-first2=Jeff |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Like Men's Studies and Masculinity Studies more generally, Critical Studies on Men has been critiqued for its failure to adequately focus on the issue of men's relations with children as a key site for the development of men's oppressive masculinity formations - men's relations with women and men's relations with other men being the two sites which are heavily researched by comparison.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-29012-6_3 |chapter=Doing (Oppressive) Gender Via Men's Relations with Children |title=Critical Perspectives on Masculinities and Relationalities |series=Crossroads of Knowledge |year=2016 |last1=Pringle |first1=Keith |pages=23–34 |isbn=978-3-319-29011-9 }}</ref>

== Topics ==

=== Masculinity ===
Early men's studies scholars studied [[Social construction of gender|social construction]] of masculinity,<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|title=The making of masculinities : the new men's studies|last=Brod|first=Harry|publisher=Allen & Unwin, Inc.|year=1987|isbn=978-1-138-82833-9|oclc=951132208}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> which the Australian sociologist [[Raewyn Connell]] is best known for.

Connell introduced the concept of [[hegemonic masculinity]], describing it as a practice that legitimizes men's dominant position in society and justifies the subordination of the common male population and women, and other marginalized ways of being a man. Being pervasive across societies,<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |journal=Gender & Society |date=December 2005 |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |s2cid=5804166 |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> it results in multiple masculinities,<ref name=":0">{{cite book|title=Masculinities|last=Connell|first=R. W.|publisher=Polity Press|year=1995|isbn=978-0-7456-1469-4|location=Cambridge, UK|author-link=R.W. Connell}}</ref> specifically a hierarchy of masculinities, in which some men do not experience the same privilege other men do, because of their other [[Social exclusion|marginalized]] identities.<ref name=":2" /> The concept has attracted several criticisms (see {{section link|Hegemonic masculinity|Criticisms}}), which led to Connell (and James Messerschmitt)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |date=2005 |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27640853 |journal=Gender and Society |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |jstor=27640853 |s2cid=5804166 |issn=0891-2432|url-access=subscription |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> reformulating areas of hegemonic masculinity. This newer version looks at the power and social dynamics found in the gender hierarchy, the geography of masculinity at local, regional, and global levels, social embodiment, and the dynamics of masculinity, including the complex interlayering of multiple masculinities.<ref name=":2" /> Connell emphasizes that masculinity is constantly evolving, meaning the curriculum and research of this field will always change.<ref name=":0" />

[[Michael Kimmel]], an American sociologist and feminist specializing in gender studies, has written about manhood in America. According to Kimmel, masculinity began to be defined and reaffirmed around 19th century America. It involved proving one's masculine worth as well as providing for one's family,<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Manhood in America: A Cultural History|last=Kimmel|first=Michael|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2006|location=New York}}</ref> and thereby also affected the political arena, workplace, family, and society at large.<ref name=":4">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/politicsofmanhoo00kimm|url-access=registration|title=The politics of manhood|publisher=[[Temple University Press]]|year=1995|isbn=978-1-56639-365-2|editor1-last=Kimmel|editor1-first=Michael|editor-link=Michael Kimmel|location=Philadelphia}}</ref> Kimmel posits that the imbibing of masculinity happens to young boys at home, at school and when watching adults interact.<ref name=":3" /> Kimmel described the term '[[toxic masculinity]]' as the male-enacted cultural norms that are harmful to men and society, because they encourage negative behaviors related to dominance, aggression and sexuality.<ref name=":4" />

[[Eric Anderson (sociologist)|Eric Anderson]], an American sociologist and sexologist specializing in adolescent men's gender and sexualities, has researched and written about the relationship between hegemonic masculinity and homophobia.<ref name=":5">{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203871485 |title=Inclusive Masculinity |year=2010 |last1=Anderson |first1=Eric |isbn=978-1-135-22717-3 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> According to Anderson's empirical research, he found that decreasing homophobia can lead to more inclusive masculinity because hegemonic masculinity has limited men's behavior in fear of being perceived as gay.<ref name=":5" /> Kimmel describes this theory as "[[Inclusive masculinity|Inclusive Masculinity Theory]]".

=== Cultural expectations ===
It has been argued that the cultural expectations of boys and men to be tough, stoic, aggressive and unemotional are harmful to men's development because they reduce the range of human [[emotion]]s being experienced, increase levels of [[anger]] and [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and can even result in a shortened life expectancy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kupers |first1=Terry A. |title=Toxic masculinity as a barrier to mental health treatment in prison |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |date=June 2005 |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=713–724 |doi=10.1002/jclp.20105 |pmid=15732090 }}</ref>

=== Violence ===
Research on [[violence]] has been a major focus of men's studies. Research focuses on men as both perpetrators and [[Violence against men|victims]] of violence, as well as on how to involve men and boys in anti-violence work.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780429280054-1 |chapter=What has masculinity to do with intimate partner violence? |title=Men, Masculinities and Intimate Partner Violence |year=2020 |last1=Gottzén |first1=Lucas |last2=Bjørnholt |first2=Margunn |last3=Boonzaier |first3=Floretta |pages=1–15 |isbn=978-0-429-28005-4 |s2cid=224922714 }}</ref>

=== Sexuality ===
Studying the relation between masculinity and male sexual shame revealed that greater endorsement of traditionally masculine values was associated with increased sexual [[shame]], and which in turn is predictive of depression.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://newmalestudies.com/OJS/index.php/nms/article/view/292/353|title=Male sexual shame, masculinity, and mental health |journal=New Male Studies|last=Gordon|first=Aqualus|date=2019-07-01|volume=8|issue=1|pages=1–24}}</ref>

=== Health ===
Men's studies scholars have studied aspects of men's health and illness<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n1 |chapter=Rethinking Men's Health and Illness: The Relevance of Gender Studies |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Sabo |first1=Donald |last2=Gordon |first2=David Frederick |pages=2–21 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref> such as premature death<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n3 |chapter=Premature Death among Males: Extending the Bottom Line of Men's Health |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Stillion |first1=Judith M. |pages=46–67 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref> and coronary heart disease.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n4 |chapter=Masculinity, Men's Roles, and Coronary Heart Disease |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Helgeson |first1=Vicki S. |pages=68–104 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref>

===Work and care===
Men's studies is notably concerned with challenging gendered arrangements of work and care, and the male breadwinner role, and policies are increasingly targeting men as fathers, as a tool of changing gender relations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bjørnholt |first1=Margunn |author-link1=Margunn Bjørnholt |title=Changing Men, Changing Times – Fathers and Sons from an Experimental Gender Equality Study |journal=The Sociological Review |date=May 2014 |volume=62 |issue=2 |pages=295–315 |doi=10.1111/1467-954X.12156 |s2cid=143048732 }}</ref>

===Boys and boyhoods===
The study of boys and boyhoods has emerged from within the sociology of [[masculinity]], and focuses on the ways that ideas and expectations around gender shape boys' experiences of childhood. For Laurie et al., "ideas about boys and boyhood have considerable currency in shaping understandings of the causes of gender inequality, and significantly impact any efforts to transform gender-based hierarchies."<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.academia.edu/111004474|title=Towards an Affirmative Feminist Boys Studies |journal=Boyhood Studies |first2=Catherine|last2=Driscoll|first3= Liam|last3= Grealy|first1=Timothy|last1=Laurie|first4=Shawna|last4=Tang|first5=Grace|last5=Sharkey|volume=14|issue=1|pages=75–92}}</ref>

== Organizations ==
The [[American Men's Studies Association]] (AMSA) traces the roots of an organized field of men's studies to the early 1980s and the work of scholars involved in an [[Sexism|anti-sexist]] organization called the Men's Studies Task Group (MSTG) of the National Organization for Changing Men (NOCM) which included Martin Acker, Shepherd Bliss, [[Harry Brod]], Sam Femiano, Martin Fiebert, and [[Michael Messner]]. However, men's studies classes also pre-date NOCM, and a small number were taught in various colleges across the United States throughout the 1970s.<ref name=":1" /> Conferences such as the Men and Masculinity conferences sparked the creation of newsletters and journals, such as the ''Men's Studies Newsletter'' (and its successor, ''Men's Studies Review''),<ref>{{cite journal | title = Men's Studies Review (journal) | journal = Men's Studies Review | publisher = American Men's Studies Association (AMSA) | location = Harriman, Tennessee | lccn = 93648850 | issn = 0890-9741}}</ref> pertaining to the growing field of men's studies. These became prime resources for those interested in the field, providing news, bibliographies, and firsthand experiences. Following the newsletters and journals came the [[Men's Studies Press]], thus moving the academic field of masculinity studies to books.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Doyle|first1=James. A|last2=Femiano|first2=Sam | title = A history of the Men's Studies Press and its Association with the American Men's Studies Association | journal = The Journal of Men's Studies| volume = 21 | issue = 1 | pages = 24–33 | doi = 10.3149/jms.2101.24 | date = January 2013 |s2cid=147376751}}

*''See also'':

:*{{cite web  |last1=Doyle|first1=James. A|last2=Femiano|first2=Sam | title = The early history of the American Men's Studies Association and the evolution of men's studies | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171010181602/http://mensstudies.org/?page_id=5 | archive-date = 10 October 2017 | url = http://mensstudies.org/?page_id=5 | website = mensstudies.org | publisher = American Men's Studies Association (AMSA) | date = 1999 | access-date = 25 November 2017 }}
</ref>

When NOCM changed its name to the [[National Organization for Men Against Sexism]] (NOMAS),<ref>{{cite web | title = Home page | url = http://www.nomas.org/ | website = nomas.org | publisher = [[National Organization for Men Against Sexism]] (NOMAS) }}</ref> the MSTG became the Men's Studies Association (MSA). The MSA was an explicitly pro-feminist group, and those who felt this was too constraining split away several years later to form the American Men's Studies Association (AMSA), although the NOMAS would not let AMSA become its own self-governing entity, which led to clashes in ideologies between the two groups.<ref name=":1" />

== Journals ==
The men and masculinities field includes at least eight focused journals: ''Culture, Society, and Masculinities'', ''Journal of Men's Studies'', ''Masculinities and Social Change'', ''Masculinities: A Journal of Identity and Culture'', ''[[Men and Masculinities]]'', ''New Male Studies'', ''[[Norma (journal)|Norma: International Journal for Masculinity Studies]]'', and ''Psychology of Men & Masculinity''.{{citation needed|date=September 2022}}

== Feminist criticism ==
The field of men's studies has received criticism due to its separative nature from the rest of [[gender studies]].

Some feminists view men's studies only as taking away potential limited funding dedicated for [[women's studies]].<ref name=":1" /> Timothy Laurie and [[Anna Hickey-Moody]] insist that "[any] atomisation of masculinity studies as distinct from gender studies, feminist inquiry or queer studies must be understood as provisional and hazardous rather than as the result of absolute differences in the phenomena being investigated or expertise required".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hickey-Moody |first1=Anna |last2=Laurie |first2=Timothy |title=Geophilosophies of masculinity: Remapping gender, aesthetics and knowledge |journal=[[Angelaki]] |date=2 January 2015 |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1080/0969725X.2015.1017359 |hdl=10453/44702 |s2cid=145472959 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Some feminists also argue that many gender and race studies were created to discuss the oppression that these race/genders experience. Since men are the primary oppressor of these, men's studies shouldn't be included within "oppression" studies because it "risks leveling structure of power by granting men's studies an equal and complementary place to women's studies".<ref name=":7">{{cite book |last1=Gardiner |first1=Judith Kegan |title=Masculinity Studies and Feminist Theory |date=2002 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-50491-1 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In 1989 Joyce E. Canaan and Christine Griffin described their suspicions of The New Men's Studies (TNMS), saying "Is it a coincidence that TNMS is being constructed in the present context as a source of potential research, publishing deals, and (even more) jobs for the already-well-paid boys holding prestigious positions?"<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Canaan | first1 = Joyce E. | last2 = Griffin | first2 = Christine | chapter = The new men's studies: part of the problem or part of the solution | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=yC5HBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA208 | editor-last1 = Morgan | editor-first1 = D. H. J. | editor-last2 = Hearn | editor-first2 = Jeff | editor-link1 = David Morgan (sociologist) | editor-link2 = Jeff Hearn | title = Men, masculinities & social theory | page = 208 | publisher = Unwin Hyman | location = London Boston | year = 1990 | isbn = 978-0-04-445658-2 }}

:''Originally published as'': {{cite journal | last1 = Canaan | first1 = Joyce E. | last2 = Griffin | first2 = Christine | title = The new men's studies: part of the problem or part of the solution | journal = [[British Sociological Association#Network newsletter|Network (newsletter)]] | volume = 43 | pages = 7–8 | date = 1985 | url = https://www.britsoc.co.uk/publications/network.aspx }}</ref> Researchers in [[transgender studies]], including [[Jack Halberstam]], have also questioned the relationship between male biology and gender identity within masculinity studies.<ref name=":7" />

Men's studies scholars have responded to this by explaining the importance of men's studies. [[Harry Brod]], an American sociologist, explains that the importance of men's studies is that prior to the emergence of the discipline, feminists had been looking at the generalization of men, whereas this discipline focuses on the "study of masculinities and male experiences as specific and varying social-historical-cultural formations."<ref name=":6" /> Connell adds that by having a field for masculinity studies it may help "identify men's interest in change".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=Robert W. |title=Understanding Men: Gender Sociology and the New International Research on Masculinities |journal=Social Thought & Research |date=2001 |volume=24 |issue=1/2 |pages=13–31 |jstor=23250072 }}</ref>

Early men's studies scholars studied [[Social construction of gender|social construction]] of masculinity,<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|title=The making of masculinities : the new men's studies|last=Brod|first=Harry|publisher=Allen & Unwin, Inc.|year=1987|isbn=978-1-138-82833-9|oclc=951132208}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> which the Australian sociologist [[Raewyn Connell]] is best known for.

Connell introduced the concept of [[hegemonic masculinity]], describing it as a practice that legitimizes men's dominant position in society and justifies the subordination of the common male population and women, and other marginalized ways of being a man. Being pervasive across societies,<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |journal=Gender & Society |date=December 2005 |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |s2cid=5804166 |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> it results in multiple masculinities,<ref name=":0">{{cite book|title=Masculinities|last=Connell|first=R. W.|publisher=Polity Press|year=1995|isbn=978-0-7456-1469-4|location=Cambridge, UK|author-link=R.W. Connell}}</ref> specifically a hierarchy of masculinities, in which some men do not experience the same privilege other men do, because of their other [[Social exclusion|marginalized]] identities.<ref name=":2" /> The concept has attracted several criticisms (see {{section link|Hegemonic masculinity|Criticisms}}), which led to Connell (and James Messerschmitt)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |date=2005 |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27640853 |journal=Gender and Society |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |jstor=27640853 |s2cid=5804166 |issn=0891-2432|url-access=subscription |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> reformulating areas of hegemonic masculinity. This newer version looks at the power and social dynamics found in the gender hierarchy, the geography of masculinity at local, regional, and global levels, social embodiment, and the dynamics of masculinity, including the complex interlayering of multiple masculinities.<ref name=":2" /> Connell emphasizes that masculinity is constantly evolving, meaning the curriculum and research of this field will always change.<ref name=":0" />

[[Michael Kimmel]], an American sociologist and feminist specializing in gender studies, has written about manhood in America. According to Kimmel, masculinity began to be defined and reaffirmed around 19th century America. It involved proving one's masculine worth as well as providing for one's family,<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Manhood in America: A Cultural History|last=Kimmel|first=Michael|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2006|location=New York}}</ref> and thereby also affected the political arena, workplace, family, and society at large.<ref name=":4">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/politicsofmanhoo00kimm|url-access=registration|title=The politics of manhood|publisher=[[Temple University Press]]|year=1995|isbn=978-1-56639-365-2|editor1-last=Kimmel|editor1-first=Michael|editor-link=Michael Kimmel|location=Philadelphia}}</ref> Kimmel posits that the imbibing of masculinity happens to young boys at home, at school and when watching adults interact.<ref name=":3" /> Kimmel described the term '[[toxic masculinity]]' as the male-enacted cultural norms that are harmful to men and society, because they encourage negative behaviors related to dominance, aggression and sexuality.<ref name=":4" />

[[Eric Anderson (sociologist)|Eric Anderson]], an American sociologist and sexologist specializing in adolescent men's gender and sexualities, has researched and written about the relationship between hegemonic masculinity and homophobia.<ref name=":5">{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203871485 |title=Inclusive Masculinity |year=2010 |last1=Anderson |first1=Eric |isbn=978-1-135-22717-3 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> According to Anderson's empirical research, he found that decreasing homophobia can lead to more inclusive masculinity because hegemonic masculinity has limited men's behavior in fear of being perceived as gay.<ref name=":5" /> Kimmel describes this theory as "[[Inclusive masculinity|Inclusive Masculinity Theory]]".

=== Cultural expectations ===
It has been argued that the cultural expectations of boys and men to be tough, stoic, aggressive and unemotional are harmful to men's development because they reduce the range of human [[emotion]]s being experienced, increase levels of [[anger]] and [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and can even result in a shortened life expectancy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kupers |first1=Terry A. |title=Toxic masculinity as a barrier to mental health treatment in prison |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |date=June 2005 |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=713–724 |doi=10.1002/jclp.20105 |pmid=15732090 }}</ref>

=== Violence ===
Research on [[violence]] has been a major focus of men's studies. Research focuses on men as both perpetrators and [[Violence against men|victims]] of violence, as well as on how to involve men and boys in anti-violence work.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780429280054-1 |chapter=What has masculinity to do with intimate partner violence? |title=Men, Masculinities and Intimate Partner Violence |year=2020 |last1=Gottzén |first1=Lucas |last2=Bjørnholt |first2=Margunn |last3=Boonzaier |first3=Floretta |pages=1–15 |isbn=978-0-429-28005-4 |s2cid=224922714 }}</ref>

=== Sexuality ===
Studying the relation between masculinity and male sexual shame revealed that greater endorsement of traditionally masculine values was associated with increased sexual [[shame]], and which in turn is predictive of depression.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://newmalestudies.com/OJS/index.php/nms/article/view/292/353|title=Male sexual shame, masculinity, and mental health |journal=New Male Studies|last=Gordon|first=Aqualus|date=2019-07-01|volume=8|issue=1|pages=1–24}}</ref>

=== Health ===
Men's studies scholars have studied aspects of men's health and illness<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n1 |chapter=Rethinking Men's Health and Illness: The Relevance of Gender Studies |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Sabo |first1=Donald |last2=Gordon |first2=David Frederick |pages=2–21 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref> such as premature death<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n3 |chapter=Premature Death among Males: Extending the Bottom Line of Men's Health |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Stillion |first1=Judith M. |pages=46–67 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref> and coronary heart disease.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n4 |chapter=Masculinity, Men's Roles, and Coronary Heart Disease |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Helgeson |first1=Vicki S. |pages=68–104 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref>

===Work and care===
Men's studies is notably concerned with challenging gendered arrangements of work and care, and the male breadwinner role, and policies are increasingly targeting men as fathers, as a tool of changing gender relations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bjørnholt |first1=Margunn |author-link1=Margunn Bjørnholt |title=Changing Men, Changing Times – Fathers and Sons from an Experimental Gender Equality Study |journal=The Sociological Review |date=May 2014 |volume=62 |issue=2 |pages=295–315 |doi=10.1111/1467-954X.12156 |s2cid=143048732 }}</ref>

===Boys and boyhoods===
The study of boys and boyhoods has emerged from within the sociology of [[masculinity]], and focuses on the ways that ideas and expectations around gender shape boys' experiences of childhood. For Laurie et al., "ideas about boys and boyhood have considerable currency in shaping understandings of the causes of gender inequality, and significantly impact any efforts to transform gender-based hierarchies."<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.academia.edu/111004474|title=Towards an Affirmative Feminist Boys Studies |journal=Boyhood Studies |first2=Catherine|last2=Driscoll|first3= Liam|last3= Grealy|first1=Timothy|last1=Laurie|first4=Shawna|last4=Tang|first5=Grace|last5=Sharkey|volume=14|issue=1|pages=75–92}}</ref>

== Organizations ==
The [[American Men's Studies Association]] (AMSA) traces the roots of an organized field of men's studies to the early 1980s and the work of scholars involved in an [[Sexism|anti-sexist]] organization called the Men's Studies Task Group (MSTG) of the National Organization for Changing Men (NOCM) which included Martin Acker, Shepherd Bliss, [[Harry Brod]], Sam Femiano, Martin Fiebert, and [[Michael Messner]]. However, men's studies classes also pre-date NOCM, and a small number were taught in various colleges across the United States throughout the 1970s.<ref name=":1" /> Conferences such as the Men and Masculinity conferences sparked the creation of newsletters and journals, such as the ''Men's Studies Newsletter'' (and its successor, ''Men's Studies Review''),<ref>{{cite journal | title = Men's Studies Review (journal) | journal = Men's Studies Review | publisher = American Men's Studies Association (AMSA) | location = Harriman, Tennessee | lccn = 93648850 | issn = 0890-9741}}</ref> pertaining to the growing field of men's studies. These became prime resources for those interested in the field, providing news, bibliographies, and firsthand experiences. Following the newsletters and journals came the [[Men's Studies Press]], thus moving the academic field of masculinity studies to books.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Doyle|first1=James. A|last2=Femiano|first2=Sam | title = A history of the Men's Studies Press and its Association with the American Men's Studies Association | journal = The Journal of Men's Studies| volume = 21 | issue = 1 | pages = 24–33 | doi = 10.3149/jms.2101.24 | date = January 2013 |s2cid=147376751}}

When NOCM changed its name to the [[National Organization for Men Against Sexism]] (NOMAS),<ref>{{cite web | title = Home page | url = http://www.nomas.org/ | website = nomas.org | publisher = [[National Organization for Men Against Sexism]] (NOMAS) }}</ref> the MSTG became the Men's Studies Association (MSA). The MSA was an explicitly pro-feminist group, and those who felt this was too constraining split away several years later to form the American Men's Studies Association (AMSA), although the NOMAS would not let AMSA become its own self-governing entity, which led to clashes in ideologies between the two groups.<ref name=":1" />

== Journals ==
The men and masculinities field includes at least eight focused journals: ''Culture, Society, and Masculinities'', ''Journal of Men's Studies'', ''Masculinities and Social Change'', ''Masculinities: A Journal of Identity and Culture'', ''[[Men and Masculinities]]'', ''New Male Studies'', ''[[Norma (journal)|Norma: International Journal for Masculinity Studies]]'', and ''Psychology of Men & Masculinity''.{{citation needed|date=September 2022}}

== Feminist criticism ==
The field of men's studies has received criticism due to its separative nature from the rest of [[gender studies]].

Some feminists view men's studies only as taking away potential limited funding dedicated for [[women's studies]].<ref name=":1" /> Timothy Laurie and [[Anna Hickey-Moody]] insist that "[any] atomisation of masculinity studies as distinct from gender studies, feminist inquiry or queer studies must be understood as provisional and hazardous rather than as the result of absolute differences in the phenomena being investigated or expertise required".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hickey-Moody |first1=Anna |last2=Laurie |first2=Timothy |title=Geophilosophies of masculinity: Remapping gender, aesthetics and knowledge |journal=[[Angelaki]] |date=2 January 2015 |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1080/0969725X.2015.1017359 |hdl=10453/44702 |s2cid=145472959 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Some feminists also argue that many gender and race studies were created to discuss the oppression that these race/genders experience. Since men are the primary oppressor of these, men's studies shouldn't be included within "oppression" studies because it "risks leveling structure of power by granting men's studies an equal and complementary place to women's studies".<ref name=":7">{{cite book |last1=Gardiner |first1=Judith Kegan |title=Masculinity Studies and Feminist Theory |date=2002 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-50491-1 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In 1989 Joyce E. Canaan and Christine Griffin described their suspicions of The New Men's Studies (TNMS), saying "Is it a coincidence that TNMS is being constructed in the present context as a source of potential research, publishing deals, and (even more) jobs for the already-well-paid boys holding prestigious positions?"<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Canaan | first1 = Joyce E. | last2 = Griffin | first2 = Christine | chapter = The new men's studies: part of the problem or part of the solution | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=yC5HBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA208 | editor-last1 = Morgan | editor-first1 = D. H. J. | editor-last2 = Hearn | editor-first2 = Jeff | editor-link1 = David Morgan (sociologist) | editor-link2 = Jeff Hearn | title = Men, masculinities & social theory | page = 208 | publisher = Unwin Hyman | location = London Boston | year = 1990 | isbn = 978-0-04-445658-2 }}

:''Originally published as'': {{cite journal | last1 = Canaan | first1 = Joyce E. | last2 = Griffin | first2 = Christine | title = The new men's studies: part of the problem or part of the solution | journal = [[British Sociological Association#Network newsletter|Network (newsletter)]] | volume = 43 | pages = 7–8 | date = 1985 | url = https://www.britsoc.co.uk/publications/network.aspx }}</ref> Researchers in [[transgender studies]], including [[Jack Halberstam]], have also questioned the relationship between male biology and gender identity within masculinity studies.<ref name=":7" />

Men's studies scholars have responded to this by explaining the importance of men's studies. [[Harry Brod]], an American sociologist, explains that the importance of men's studies is that prior to the emergence of the discipline, feminists had been looking at the generalization of men, whereas this discipline focuses on the "study of masculinities and male experiences as specific and varying social-historical-cultural formations."<ref name=":6" /> Connell adds that by having a field for masculinity studies it may help "identify men's interest in change".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=Robert W. |title=Understanding Men: Gender Sociology and the New International Research on Masculinities |journal=Social Thought & Research |date=2001 |volume=24 |issue=1/2 |pages=13–31 |jstor=23250072 }}</ref>

'''Men's studies''' is an [[interdisciplinary]] [[academic field]] devoted to topics concerning [[men]], [[masculinity]], [[gender]], [[culture]], [[politics]] and [[Human sexuality|sexuality]]. It academically examines what it means to be a man in contemporary society.<ref>{{Cite news |last= Bennett|first=Jessica |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/09/fashion/masculinities-studies-stonybrook-michael-kimmel.html?_r=0|title=A master's degree in...masculinity?|date=August 8, 2015|work=[[New York Times]]}}</ref>

== Origins ==
Sociologists and psychologists in the [[Nordic countries]] such as Norwegians [[Erik Grønseth]] and [[Per Olav Tiller]] were early pioneers of men's studies as a research field; Grønseth and Tiller's classic study of [[father absence]] in sailor families and its impact on children's [[personality development]] in the 1950s is often regarded as the starting point of men's studies in the Nordic countries.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Mannsforskning |encyclopedia=[[Store norske leksikon]] |year=2018 |url=https://snl.no/mannsforskning }}</ref>

In Anglophone countries, men's studies was formed, largely in response to an emerging [[men's rights]] movement,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wootton |first1=Nancy A. |title=The men's movement and men's studies: a study of the literature |journal=RQ |date=Winter 1993 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=183–194 |id={{Gale|A14769920}} |jstor=20862406 }}</ref> and as such, has been taught in academic settings only since the 1970s.<ref name=":1" />
 
In contrast to the discipline of masculine psychology, men's studies programs and courses often include contemporary discussions of men's rights, [[feminist theory]], [[queer theory]], [[matriarchy]], [[patriarchy]], and more generally, what proponents describe as the social, historical, and cultural influences on the constructions of [[Man|men]]. They often discuss the issues surrounding [[male privilege]], seen as evolving into more subtle and covert forms rather than disappearing in the modern era.{{Citation needed|date=February 2020}}

It is important to distinguish the specific approach often defined as Critical Studies on Men. This approach was largely developed in the anglophone countries from the early 1980s - especially in the United Kingdom -  centred then around the work of Jeff Hearn, David Morgan and colleagues.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book|editor1=Hearn, Jeff |editor2=Morgan, David|title=Men, masculinities & social theory|publisher=Unwin Hyman|year=1990|location=London}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> The influence of the approach has spread globally since then. It is inspired primarily by a range of feminist perspectives (including socialist and radical) and places emphasis on the need for research and practice to explicitly challenge men's and boys' sexism.<ref name=":8" /> Although it explores a very broad range of men's practices, it tends to focus especially on issues related to sexuality and/or men's violences.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=The Violences of Men: How Men Talk About and How Agencies Respond to Men's Violence to Women |date=1998 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-0-8039-7940-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Although originally largely rooted in sociology, it has since engaged with a broad range of other disciplines including social policy, social work, cultural studies, gender studies, education and law.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203413067 |title=International Encyclopedia of Men and Masculinities |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-134-31707-3 |editor-last1=Flood |editor-last2=Kegan Gardiner |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Michael |editor-first2=Judith |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In more recent years, Critical Studies on Men research has made particular use of comparative and/or transnational perspectives.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=Men of the World: Genders, Globalizations, Transnational Times |date=2015 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-1-4739-2677-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230626447 |title=European Perspectives on Men and Masculinities |year=2006 |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |last2=Pringle |first2=Keith |isbn=978-0-230-59447-0 |url=http://www.palgrave.com/us/book/9781403918130 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230338005 |title=Men and Masculinities Around the World |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-349-29067-3 |editor-last1=Ruspini |editor-last2=Hearn |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Elisabetta |editor-first2=Jeff |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Like Men's Studies and Masculinity Studies more generally, Critical Studies on Men has been critiqued for its failure to adequately focus on the issue of men's relations with children as a key site for the development of men's oppressive masculinity formations - men's relations with women and men's relations with other men being the two sites which are heavily researched by comparison.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-29012-6_3 |chapter=Doing (Oppressive) Gender Via Men's Relations with Children |title=Critical Perspectives on Masculinities and Relationalities |series=Crossroads of Knowledge |year=2016 |last1=Pringle |first1=Keith |pages=23–34 |isbn=978-3-319-29011-9 }}</ref>

Studying the relation between masculinity and male sexual shame revealed that greater endorsement of traditionally masculine values was associated with increased sexual [[shame]], and which in turn is predictive of depression.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://newmalestudies.com/OJS/index.php/nms/article/view/292/353|title=Male sexual shame, masculinity, and mental health |journal=New Male Studies|last=Gordon|first=Aqualus|date=2019-07-01|volume=8|issue=1|pages=1–24}}</ref>

A|last2=Femiano|first2=Sam | title = A history of the Men's Studies Press and its Association with the American Men's Studies Association | journal = The Journal of Men's Studies| volume = 21 | issue = 1 | pages = 24–33 | doi = 10.3149/jms.2101.24 | date = January 2013 |s2cid=147376751}}

The men and masculinities field includes at least eight focused journals: ''Culture, Society, and Masculinities'', ''Journal of Men's Studies'', ''Masculinities and Social Change'', ''Masculinities: A Journal of Identity and Culture'', ''[[Men and Masculinities]]'', ''New Male Studies'', ''[[Norma (journal)|Norma: International Journal for Masculinity Studies]]'', and ''Psychology of Men & Masculinity''.{{citation needed|date=September 2022}}

The field of men's studies has received criticism due to its separative nature from the rest of [[gender studies]].

Some feminists view men's studies only as taking away potential limited funding dedicated for [[women's studies]].<ref name=":1" /> Timothy Laurie and [[Anna Hickey-Moody]] insist that "[any] atomisation of masculinity studies as distinct from gender studies, feminist inquiry or queer studies must be understood as provisional and hazardous rather than as the result of absolute differences in the phenomena being investigated or expertise required".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hickey-Moody |first1=Anna |last2=Laurie |first2=Timothy |title=Geophilosophies of masculinity: Remapping gender, aesthetics and knowledge |journal=[[Angelaki]] |date=2 January 2015 |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1080/0969725X.2015.1017359 |hdl=10453/44702 |s2cid=145472959 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Some feminists also argue that many gender and race studies were created to discuss the oppression that these race/genders experience. Since men are the primary oppressor of these, men's studies shouldn't be included within "oppression" studies because it "risks leveling structure of power by granting men's studies an equal and complementary place to women's studies".<ref name=":7">{{cite book |last1=Gardiner |first1=Judith Kegan |title=Masculinity Studies and Feminist Theory |date=2002 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-50491-1 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In 1989 Joyce E. Canaan and Christine Griffin described their suspicions of The New Men's Studies (TNMS), saying "Is it a coincidence that TNMS is being constructed in the present context as a source of potential research, publishing deals, and (even more) jobs for the already-well-paid boys holding prestigious positions?"<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Canaan | first1 = Joyce E. | last2 = Griffin | first2 = Christine | chapter = The new men's studies: part of the problem or part of the solution | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=yC5HBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA208 | editor-last1 = Morgan | editor-first1 = D. H. J. | editor-last2 = Hearn | editor-first2 = Jeff | editor-link1 = David Morgan (sociologist) | editor-link2 = Jeff Hearn | title = Men, masculinities & social theory | page = 208 | publisher = Unwin Hyman | location = London Boston | year = 1990 | isbn = 978-0-04-445658-2 }}

:''Originally published as'': {{cite journal | last1 = Canaan | first1 = Joyce E. | last2 = Griffin | first2 = Christine | title = The new men's studies: part of the problem or part of the solution | journal = [[British Sociological Association#Network newsletter|Network (newsletter)]] | volume = 43 | pages = 7–8 | date = 1985 | url = https://www.britsoc.co.uk/publications/network.aspx }}</ref> Researchers in [[transgender studies]], including [[Jack Halberstam]], have also questioned the relationship between male biology and gender identity within masculinity studies.<ref name=":7" />

'''Men's studies''' is an [[interdisciplinary]] [[academic field]] devoted to topics concerning [[men]], [[masculinity]], [[gender]], [[culture]], [[politics]] and [[Human sexuality|sexuality]]. It academically examines what it means to be a man in contemporary society.<ref>{{Cite news |last= Bennett|first=Jessica |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/09/fashion/masculinities-studies-stonybrook-michael-kimmel.html?_r=0|title=A master's degree in...masculinity?|date=August 8, 2015|work=[[New York Times]]}}</ref>

== Origins ==
Sociologists and psychologists in the [[Nordic countries]] such as Norwegians [[Erik Grønseth]] and [[Per Olav Tiller]] were early pioneers of men's studies as a research field; Grønseth and Tiller's classic study of [[father absence]] in sailor families and its impact on children's [[personality development]] in the 1950s is often regarded as the starting point of men's studies in the Nordic countries.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Mannsforskning |encyclopedia=[[Store norske leksikon]] |year=2018 |url=https://snl.no/mannsforskning }}</ref>

In Anglophone countries, men's studies was formed, largely in response to an emerging [[men's rights]] movement,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wootton |first1=Nancy A. |title=The men's movement and men's studies: a study of the literature |journal=RQ |date=Winter 1993 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=183–194 |id={{Gale|A14769920}} |jstor=20862406 }}</ref> and as such, has been taught in academic settings only since the 1970s.<ref name=":1" />
 
In contrast to the discipline of masculine psychology, men's studies programs and courses often include contemporary discussions of men's rights, [[feminist theory]], [[queer theory]], [[matriarchy]], [[patriarchy]], and more generally, what proponents describe as the social, historical, and cultural influences on the constructions of [[Man|men]]. They often discuss the issues surrounding [[male privilege]], seen as evolving into more subtle and covert forms rather than disappearing in the modern era.{{Citation needed|date=February 2020}}

It is important to distinguish the specific approach often defined as Critical Studies on Men. This approach was largely developed in the anglophone countries from the early 1980s - especially in the United Kingdom -  centred then around the work of Jeff Hearn, David Morgan and colleagues.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book|editor1=Hearn, Jeff |editor2=Morgan, David|title=Men, masculinities & social theory|publisher=Unwin Hyman|year=1990|location=London}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> The influence of the approach has spread globally since then. It is inspired primarily by a range of feminist perspectives (including socialist and radical) and places emphasis on the need for research and practice to explicitly challenge men's and boys' sexism.<ref name=":8" /> Although it explores a very broad range of men's practices, it tends to focus especially on issues related to sexuality and/or men's violences.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=The Violences of Men: How Men Talk About and How Agencies Respond to Men's Violence to Women |date=1998 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-0-8039-7940-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Although originally largely rooted in sociology, it has since engaged with a broad range of other disciplines including social policy, social work, cultural studies, gender studies, education and law.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203413067 |title=International Encyclopedia of Men and Masculinities |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-134-31707-3 |editor-last1=Flood |editor-last2=Kegan Gardiner |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Michael |editor-first2=Judith |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In more recent years, Critical Studies on Men research has made particular use of comparative and/or transnational perspectives.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=Men of the World: Genders, Globalizations, Transnational Times |date=2015 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-1-4739-2677-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230626447 |title=European Perspectives on Men and Masculinities |year=2006 |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |last2=Pringle |first2=Keith |isbn=978-0-230-59447-0 |url=http://www.palgrave.com/us/book/9781403918130 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230338005 |title=Men and Masculinities Around the World |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-349-29067-3 |editor-last1=Ruspini |editor-last2=Hearn |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Elisabetta |editor-first2=Jeff |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Like Men's Studies and Masculinity Studies more generally, Critical Studies on Men has been critiqued for its failure to adequately focus on the issue of men's relations with children as a key site for the development of men's oppressive masculinity formations - men's relations with women and men's relations with other men being the two sites which are heavily researched by comparison.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-29012-6_3 |chapter=Doing (Oppressive) Gender Via Men's Relations with Children |title=Critical Perspectives on Masculinities and Relationalities |series=Crossroads of Knowledge |year=2016 |last1=Pringle |first1=Keith |pages=23–34 |isbn=978-3-319-29011-9 }}</ref>

=== Masculinity ===
Early men's studies scholars studied [[Social construction of gender|social construction]] of masculinity,<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|title=The making of masculinities : the new men's studies|last=Brod|first=Harry|publisher=Allen & Unwin, Inc.|year=1987|isbn=978-1-138-82833-9|oclc=951132208}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> which the Australian sociologist [[Raewyn Connell]] is best known for.

Connell introduced the concept of [[hegemonic masculinity]], describing it as a practice that legitimizes men's dominant position in society and justifies the subordination of the common male population and women, and other marginalized ways of being a man. Being pervasive across societies,<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |journal=Gender & Society |date=December 2005 |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |s2cid=5804166 |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> it results in multiple masculinities,<ref name=":0">{{cite book|title=Masculinities|last=Connell|first=R. W.|publisher=Polity Press|year=1995|isbn=978-0-7456-1469-4|location=Cambridge, UK|author-link=R.W. Connell}}</ref> specifically a hierarchy of masculinities, in which some men do not experience the same privilege other men do, because of their other [[Social exclusion|marginalized]] identities.<ref name=":2" /> The concept has attracted several criticisms (see {{section link|Hegemonic masculinity|Criticisms}}), which led to Connell (and James Messerschmitt)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |date=2005 |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27640853 |journal=Gender and Society |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |jstor=27640853 |s2cid=5804166 |issn=0891-2432|url-access=subscription |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> reformulating areas of hegemonic masculinity. This newer version looks at the power and social dynamics found in the gender hierarchy, the geography of masculinity at local, regional, and global levels, social embodiment, and the dynamics of masculinity, including the complex interlayering of multiple masculinities.<ref name=":2" /> Connell emphasizes that masculinity is constantly evolving, meaning the curriculum and research of this field will always change.<ref name=":0" />

[[Michael Kimmel]], an American sociologist and feminist specializing in gender studies, has written about manhood in America. According to Kimmel, masculinity began to be defined and reaffirmed around 19th century America. It involved proving one's masculine worth as well as providing for one's family,<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Manhood in America: A Cultural History|last=Kimmel|first=Michael|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2006|location=New York}}</ref> and thereby also affected the political arena, workplace, family, and society at large.<ref name=":4">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/politicsofmanhoo00kimm|url-access=registration|title=The politics of manhood|publisher=[[Temple University Press]]|year=1995|isbn=978-1-56639-365-2|editor1-last=Kimmel|editor1-first=Michael|editor-link=Michael Kimmel|location=Philadelphia}}</ref> Kimmel posits that the imbibing of masculinity happens to young boys at home, at school and when watching adults interact.<ref name=":3" /> Kimmel described the term '[[toxic masculinity]]' as the male-enacted cultural norms that are harmful to men and society, because they encourage negative behaviors related to dominance, aggression and sexuality.<ref name=":4" />

[[Eric Anderson (sociologist)|Eric Anderson]], an American sociologist and sexologist specializing in adolescent men's gender and sexualities, has researched and written about the relationship between hegemonic masculinity and homophobia.<ref name=":5">{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203871485 |title=Inclusive Masculinity |year=2010 |last1=Anderson |first1=Eric |isbn=978-1-135-22717-3 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> According to Anderson's empirical research, he found that decreasing homophobia can lead to more inclusive masculinity because hegemonic masculinity has limited men's behavior in fear of being perceived as gay.<ref name=":5" /> Kimmel describes this theory as "[[Inclusive masculinity|Inclusive Masculinity Theory]]".

Since men are the primary oppressor of these, men's studies shouldn't be included within "oppression" studies because it "risks leveling structure of power by granting men's studies an equal and complementary place to women's studies".<ref name=":7">{{cite book |last1=Gardiner |first1=Judith Kegan |title=Masculinity Studies and Feminist Theory |date=2002 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=978-0-231-50491-1 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In 1989 Joyce E. Canaan and Christine Griffin described their suspicions of The New Men's Studies (TNMS), saying "Is it a coincidence that TNMS is being constructed in the present context as a source of potential research, publishing deals, and (even more) jobs for the already-well-paid boys holding prestigious positions?"<ref>{{cite book | last1 = Canaan | first1 = Joyce E. | last2 = Griffin | first2 = Christine | chapter = The new men's studies: part of the problem or part of the solution | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=yC5HBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA208 | editor-last1 = Morgan | editor-first1 = D. H. J. | editor-last2 = Hearn | editor-first2 = Jeff | editor-link1 = David Morgan (sociologist) | editor-link2 = Jeff Hearn | title = Men, masculinities & social theory | page = 208 | publisher = Unwin Hyman | location = London Boston | year = 1990 | isbn = 978-0-04-445658-2 }}

Men's studies scholars have responded to this by explaining the importance of men's studies. {{Short description|Interdisciplinary academic field}}
{{Lead too short|date=August 2021}}

'''Men's studies''' is an [[interdisciplinary]] [[academic field]] devoted to topics concerning [[men]], [[masculinity]], [[gender]], [[culture]], [[politics]] and [[Human sexuality|sexuality]]. It academically examines what it means to be a man in contemporary society.<ref>{{Cite news |last= Bennett|first=Jessica |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/09/fashion/masculinities-studies-stonybrook-michael-kimmel.html?_r=0|title=A master's degree in...masculinity?|date=August 8, 2015|work=[[New York Times]]}}</ref>

== Origins ==
{{More citations needed section|date=February 2020}}
Sociologists and psychologists in the [[Nordic countries]] such as Norwegians [[Erik Grønseth]] and [[Per Olav Tiller]] were early pioneers of men's studies as a research field; Grønseth and Tiller's classic study of [[father absence]] in sailor families and its impact on children's [[personality development]] in the 1950s is often regarded as the starting point of men's studies in the Nordic countries.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |title=Mannsforskning |encyclopedia=[[Store norske leksikon]] |year=2018 |url=https://snl.no/mannsforskning }}</ref>

In Anglophone countries, men's studies was formed, largely in response to an emerging [[men's rights]] movement,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wootton |first1=Nancy A. |title=The men's movement and men's studies: a study of the literature |journal=RQ |date=Winter 1993 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=183–194 |id={{Gale|A14769920}} |jstor=20862406 }}</ref> and as such, has been taught in academic settings only since the 1970s.<ref name=":1" />
 
In contrast to the discipline of masculine psychology, men's studies programs and courses often include contemporary discussions of men's rights, [[feminist theory]], [[queer theory]], [[matriarchy]], [[patriarchy]], and more generally, what proponents describe as the social, historical, and cultural influences on the constructions of [[Man|men]]. They often discuss the issues surrounding [[male privilege]], seen as evolving into more subtle and covert forms rather than disappearing in the modern era.{{Citation needed|date=February 2020}}

It is important to distinguish the specific approach often defined as Critical Studies on Men. This approach was largely developed in the anglophone countries from the early 1980s - especially in the United Kingdom -  centred then around the work of Jeff Hearn, David Morgan and colleagues.<ref name=":8">{{Cite book|last=Hearn, Jeff and Morgan, David|title=Men, masculinities & social theory|publisher=Unwin Hyman|year=1990|isbn=|location=London|pages=}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> The influence of the approach has spread globally since then. It is inspired primarily by a range of feminist perspectives (including socialist and radical) and places emphasis on the need for research and practice to explicitly challenge men's and boys' sexism.<ref name=":8" /> Although it explores a very broad range of men's practices, it tends to focus especially on issues related to sexuality and/or men's violences.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=The Violences of Men: How Men Talk About and How Agencies Respond to Men's Violence to Women |date=1998 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-0-8039-7940-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Although originally largely rooted in sociology, it has since engaged with a broad range of other disciplines including social policy, social work, cultural studies, gender studies, education and law.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203413067 |title=International Encyclopedia of Men and Masculinities |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-134-31707-3 |editor-last1=Flood |editor-last2=Kegan Gardiner |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Michael |editor-first2=Judith |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> In more recent years, Critical Studies on Men research has made particular use of comparative and/or transnational perspectives.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |title=Men of the World: Genders, Globalizations, Transnational Times |date=2015 |publisher=SAGE |isbn=978-1-4739-2677-6 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230626447 |title=European Perspectives on Men and Masculinities |year=2006 |last1=Hearn |first1=Jeff |last2=Pringle |first2=Keith |isbn=978-0-230-59447-0 |url=http://www.palgrave.com/us/book/9781403918130 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1057/9780230338005 |title=Men and Masculinities Around the World |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-349-29067-3 |editor-last1=Ruspini |editor-last2=Hearn |editor-last3=Pease |editor-last4=Pringle |editor-first1=Elisabetta |editor-first2=Jeff |editor-first3=Bob |editor-first4=Keith }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> Like Men's Studies and Masculinity Studies more generally, Critical Studies on Men has been critiqued for its failure to adequately focus on the issue of men's relations with children as a key site for the development of men's oppressive masculinity formations - men's relations with women and men's relations with other men being the two sites which are heavily researched by comparison.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-29012-6_3 |chapter=Doing (Oppressive) Gender Via Men's Relations with Children |title=Critical Perspectives on Masculinities and Relationalities |series=Crossroads of Knowledge |year=2016 |last1=Pringle |first1=Keith |pages=23–34 |isbn=978-3-319-29011-9 }}</ref>

== Topics ==

=== Masculinity ===
Early men's studies scholars studied [[Social construction of gender|social construction]] of masculinity,<ref name=":6">{{Cite book|title=The making of masculinities : the new men's studies|last=Brod|first=Harry|publisher=Allen & Unwin, Inc.|year=1987|isbn=978-1-138-82833-9|oclc=951132208}}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> which the Australian sociologist [[Raewyn Connell]] is best known for.

Connell introduced the concept of [[hegemonic masculinity]], describing it as a practice that legitimizes men's dominant position in society and justifies the subordination of the common male population and women, and other marginalized ways of being a man. Being pervasive across societies,<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |journal=Gender & Society |date=December 2005 |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |s2cid=5804166 |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> it results in multiple masculinities,<ref name=":0">{{cite book|title=Masculinities|last=Connell|first=R. W.|publisher=Polity Press|year=1995|isbn=978-0-7456-1469-4|location=Cambridge, UK|author-link=R.W. Connell}}</ref> specifically a hierarchy of masculinities, in which some men do not experience the same privilege other men do, because of their other [[Social exclusion|marginalized]] identities.<ref name=":2" /> The concept has attracted several criticisms (see {{section link|Hegemonic masculinity|Criticisms}}), which led to Connell (and James Messerschmitt)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Connell |first1=R. W. |last2=Messerschmidt |first2=James W. |date=2005 |title=Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27640853 |journal=Gender and Society |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=829–859 |doi=10.1177/0891243205278639 |jstor=27640853 |s2cid=5804166 |issn=0891-2432|url-access=subscription |hdl=10818/31547 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> reformulating areas of hegemonic masculinity. This newer version looks at the power and social dynamics found in the gender hierarchy, the geography of masculinity at local, regional, and global levels, social embodiment, and the dynamics of masculinity, including the complex interlayering of multiple masculinities.<ref name=":2" /> Connell emphasizes that masculinity is constantly evolving, meaning the curriculum and research of this field will always change.<ref name=":0" />

[[Michael Kimmel]], an American sociologist and feminist specializing in gender studies, has written about manhood in America. According to Kimmel, masculinity began to be defined and reaffirmed around 19th century America. It involved proving one's masculine worth as well as providing for one's family,<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|title=Manhood in America: A Cultural History|last=Kimmel|first=Michael|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2006|location=New York}}</ref> and thereby also affected the political arena, workplace, family, and society at large.<ref name=":4">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/politicsofmanhoo00kimm|url-access=registration|title=The politics of manhood|publisher=[[Temple University Press]]|year=1995|isbn=978-1-56639-365-2|editor1-last=Kimmel|editor1-first=Michael|editor-link=Michael Kimmel|location=Philadelphia}}</ref> Kimmel posits that the imbibing of masculinity happens to young boys at home, at school and when watching adults interact.<ref name=":3" /> Kimmel described the term '[[toxic masculinity]]' as the male-enacted cultural norms that are harmful to men and society, because they encourage negative behaviors related to dominance, aggression and sexuality.<ref name=":4" />

[[Eric Anderson (sociologist)|Eric Anderson]], an American sociologist and sexologist specializing in adolescent men's gender and sexualities, has researched and written about the relationship between hegemonic masculinity and homophobia.<ref name=":5">{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203871485 |title=Inclusive Masculinity |year=2010 |last1=Anderson |first1=Eric |isbn=978-1-135-22717-3 }}{{page needed|date=September 2022}}</ref> According to Anderson's empirical research, he found that decreasing homophobia can lead to more inclusive masculinity because hegemonic masculinity has limited men's behavior in fear of being perceived as gay.<ref name=":5" /> Kimmel describes this theory as "[[Inclusive masculinity|Inclusive Masculinity Theory]]".

=== Cultural expectations ===
It has been argued that the cultural expectations of boys and men to be tough, stoic, aggressive and unemotional are harmful to men's development because they reduce the range of human [[emotion]]s being experienced, increase levels of [[anger]] and [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and can even result in a shortened life expectancy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kupers |first1=Terry A. |title=Toxic masculinity as a barrier to mental health treatment in prison |journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology |date=June 2005 |volume=61 |issue=6 |pages=713–724 |doi=10.1002/jclp.20105 |pmid=15732090 }}</ref>

=== Violence ===
Research on [[violence]] has been a major focus of men's studies. Research focuses on men as both perpetrators and [[Violence against men|victims]] of violence, as well as on how to involve men and boys in anti-violence work.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780429280054-1 |chapter=What has masculinity to do with intimate partner violence? |title=Men, Masculinities and Intimate Partner Violence |year=2020 |last1=Gottzén |first1=Lucas |last2=Bjørnholt |first2=Margunn |last3=Boonzaier |first3=Floretta |pages=1–15 |isbn=978-0-429-28005-4 |s2cid=224922714 }}</ref>

=== Sexuality ===
Studying the relation between masculinity and male sexual shame revealed that greater endorsement of traditionally masculine values was associated with increased sexual [[shame]], and which in turn is predictive of depression.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://newmalestudies.com/OJS/index.php/nms/article/view/292/353|title=Male sexual shame, masculinity, and mental health |journal=New Male Studies|last=Gordon|first=Aqualus|date=2019-07-01|volume=8|issue=1|pages=1–24}}</ref>

=== Health ===
Men's studies scholars have studied aspects of men's health and illness<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n1 |chapter=Rethinking Men's Health and Illness: The Relevance of Gender Studies |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Sabo |first1=Donald |last2=Gordon |first2=David Frederick |pages=2–21 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref> such as premature death<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n3 |chapter=Premature Death among Males: Extending the Bottom Line of Men's Health |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Stillion |first1=Judith M. |pages=46–67 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref> and coronary heart disease.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4135/9781452243757.n4 |chapter=Masculinity, Men's Roles, and Coronary Heart Disease |title=Men's Health and Illness: Gender, Power, and the Body |year=1995 |last1=Helgeson |first1=Vicki S. |pages=68–104 |isbn=978-0-8039-5275-1 }}</ref>

===Work and care===
Men's studies is notably concerned with challenging gendered arrangements of work and care, and the male breadwinner role, and policies are increasingly targeting men as fathers, as a tool of changing gender relations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bjørnholt |first1=Margunn |author-link1=Margunn Bjørnholt |title=Changing Men, Changing Times – Fathers and Sons from an Experimental Gender Equality Study |journal=The Sociological Review |date=May 2014 |volume=62 |issue=2 |pages=295–315 |doi=10.1111/1467-954X.12156 |s2cid=143048732 }}</ref>

===Boys and boyhoods===
The study of boys and boyhoods has emerged from within the sociology of [[masculinity]], and focuses on the ways that ideas and expectations around gender shape boys' experiences of childhood. For Laurie et al., "ideas about boys and boyhood have considerable currency in shaping understandings of the causes of gender inequality, and significantly impact any efforts to transform gender-based hierarchies."<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.academia.edu/111004474|title=Towards an Affirmative Feminist Boys Studies |journal=Boyhood Studies |first2=Catherine|last2=Driscoll|first3= Liam|last3= Grealy|first1=Timothy|last1=Laurie|first4=Shawna|last4=Tang|first5=Grace|last5=Sharkey|volume=14|issue=1|pages=75–92}}</ref>

The [[American Men's Studies Association]] (AMSA) traces the roots of an organized field of men's studies to the early 1980s and the work of scholars involved in an [[Sexism|anti-sexist]] organization called the Men's Studies Task Group (MSTG) of the National Organization for Changing Men (NOCM) which included Martin Acker, Shepherd Bliss, [[Harry Brod]], Sam Femiano, Martin Fiebert, and [[Michael Messner]].
